chunks: Muhammad b. Ahmad al-Sinani al-Mukattab (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: Muhammad b. Abi Abdillah al-Kufi narrated to us. He said: Sahl b. Ziyad al-Adami narrated to us from Abd al-Azim b. Abdillah al-Hasani from Imam Ali b. Muhammad from Abu Muhammad b. Ali from his father al-Rida Ali b. Musa (peace be upon them). He said:

Abu Hanifa departed one day from the presence of al-Sadiq (peace be upon him), and Musa b. Ja'far (peace be upon him) encountered him. So he said to him: O young man, from whom does sin originate? He replied: It does not go beyond three possibilities: Either it is from God, the Mighty and Majestic, and it is not from Him, for it is not proper for the Generous One to punish His servant for what he did not commit; or it is from God, the Mighty and Majestic, and from the servant, and it is not proper for the strong partner to oppress the weak partner; or it is from the servant, and indeed it is from him, so if God punishes him, it is for his sin, and if He forgives him, it is by His generosity and munificence.

key_terms.الاختيار: free will (ikhtiyar) — the capacity of humans to choose their own actions
key_terms.الجبر: compulsion (jabr) — the rejected doctrine that God forces humans to sin
key_terms.الجود: munificence (jud) — God's abundant generosity in pardoning the servant
key_terms.الشريك: partner (sharik) — used in the trilemma to show the absurdity of shared responsibility for sin
key_terms.العدل الإلهي: divine justice ('adl) — the Shia theological principle that God is just and does not oppress
key_terms.العفو: forgiveness ('afw) — God's pardon of sins committed by the servant
key_terms.الكرم: generosity (karam) — a divine attribute, the basis for God's forgiveness
key_terms.الكريم: the Generous One (al-Karim) — a divine attribute emphasizing God's generosity precludes unjust punishment
key_terms.المعصية: sin (ma'siya) — disobedience to God, the central concept debated in this hadith

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic view on free will and predestination?
ai.summary: This hadith records a famous theological exchange between the young Imam Musa ibn Ja'far al-Kadhim and the prominent Sunni jurist Abu Hanifa. After Abu Hanifa departed from Imam al-Sadiq's gathering, he encountered the young Musa and posed the question of who is responsible for human sin. The Imam presented an elegant trilemma: (1) If sin comes solely from God, then God—being the Generous One—would be unjust to punish the servant for something he did not commit; (2) If sin comes jointly from God and the servant, then the stronger partner would be oppressing the weaker one; (3) Therefore, sin must come solely from the servant, and God's punishment is deserved while His forgiveness stems from generosity. This argument represents the Shia theological position on divine justice (adl), affirming human free will and rejecting both compulsion (jabr) and delegation (tafwid).
